Empirical Research Plan: How Much Do Households Pay to Avoid a Nearby Sex-Offender?

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
   Method: Difference-in-Differences (DiD) implemented as an event-study in
   calendar time relative to the offender’s move-in date.

   Why appropriate?  
   • The registry supplies precise move-in dates → clean “shock” to local
     crime risk that is plausibly exogenous to the housing market once the
     offender has chosen a neighborhood.  
   • Rich panel of home sales prices before and after each shock allows
     property- and time-fixed effects, controlling for time-invariant
     hedonic traits and county-wide price trends.  
   • Spatial gradients (distance rings) let us use very near homes as
     “treated” and slightly farther homes in the same micro-housing market
     as contemporaneous controls, absorbing common trends and macro shocks.

   Optional complement: A spatial RD (distance to offender with a cutoff at
   0.1 mile) could be layered on the DiD (“dif-in-dif-in-dist”), but the
   primary design is a staggered DiD/event study.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  

   a. Unit of observation  
      Single-family home sale i in neighborhood n at calendar month t.

   b. Treatment variable  
      Treated_it  = 1 if sale i occurs within 0.10 mile (528 ft) of an
      offender’s address *and* after that offender’s recorded move-in date;
      0 otherwise.

      Variation comes from (i) distance and (ii) time relative to move-in.

   c. Control group  
      • Primary: Homes 0.10–0.30 mile from the same offender’s address.  
      • Secondary robustness: Homes 0.10–0.50 mile or matched houses in
        other Mecklenburg neighborhoods without a new offender in ±24 months.

   d. Treatment timing / event date  
      OffenderMoveDate_j for offender j.  For each sale we compute
      EventTime_ijt = months(sale_date – OffenderMoveDate_j).

   e. No RDD running variable needed in baseline; distance enters as
      treatment definition and/or flexible spline in robustness checks.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  

   A1. Parallel trends  
       In the absence of an offender arrival, sales prices within 0.1 mile
       and 0.10–0.30 mile of the address would have followed the same trend.
       Plausibility: Offender’s precise street choice is idiosyncratic
       conditional on neighborhood; micro-location price trends over short
       horizons are usually smooth.  We will test via pre-period event-study
       coefficients.

   A2. No anticipatory price effects before public registry update  
       Buyers/sellers only learn of the offender when the move-in is
       registered.  Given 10-day legal requirement and felony penalties,
       anticipation should be minimal.  We test for pre-trend breaks.

   A3. Stable composition of the housing stock (no endogenous renovation,
       selective listing, or bunching of transactions induced by offender)  
       Short 48-month window, property fixed effects, and balance tests
       mitigate concern; we will also check listing volume.

   A4. Spillovers limited to ≤0.30 mile  
       Farther-ring controls assumed unaffected.  Robustness with rings
       0.30–0.50 mile will be conducted.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & RESPONSES  

   T1. Offender chooses cheaper/declining blocks (location endogeneity).  
       • Use property fixed effects where we observe multiple sales of the
         same house (repeat-sales subset).  
       • Include rich baseline hedonic controls + neighborhood×year FE.  
       • Restrict to offenders who move within a neighborhood already chosen
         (spatially narrow); any block choice is plausibly idiosyncratic.

   T2. Differential time trends within very small radii (gentrification of
       certain streets).  
       • Event-study pre-period coefficients plotted; lack of trend break
         = support.  
       • Flexible neighborhood×quarter FE absorbs micro-market shocks.

   T3. Market liquidity effects (offender reduces probability of sale rather
       than price).  
       • Estimate effect on log(time-on-market) and sale probability using
         assessor data on all parcels.  
       • Show price effects hold conditional on listing.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

5. R CODE OUTLINE  

```r
# ---------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)   # fast data manipulation
library(sf)           # spatial functions
library(fixest)       # fast high-dim FE estimations
library(ggplot2)

# ---------------------------------------------
# 1. Load Data
sales  <- fread("meck_sales_1994_2004.csv")      # sale_id, parcel_id, sale_date, price
parcels<- fread("meck_parcels_2005.csv")         # parcel_id, lat, lon, hedonic vars
so      <- fread("nc_sex_offenders_2005.csv")    # offender_id, move_date, lat, lon

# ---------------------------------------------
# 2. Merge & Construct Distances
# Convert to sf for distance calc (projected CRS in feet)
sales_sf   <- st_as_sf(merge(sales, parcels, by="parcel_id"),
                       coords=c("lon","lat"), crs=4326) |> 
              st_transform(2264)         # NC State Plane (feet)

so_sf      <- st_as_sf(so, coords=c("lon","lat"), crs=4326) |> 
              st_transform(2264)

# Cartesian join to compute distance to nearest offender
dist_mat <- st_distance(sales_sf, so_sf)    # large but manageable
min_dist <- apply(dist_mat,1,min)
sales_sf$dist_ft     <- as.numeric(min_dist)
nearest_id           <- max.col(-dist_mat)  # offender index with min dist
sales_sf$offender_id <- so$offender_id[nearest_id]

# ---------------------------------------------
# 3. Relative Time Variables
sales_dt  <- as.data.table(sales_sf)
sales_dt  <- merge(sales_dt, so[,.(offender_id, move_date)], by="offender_id")
sales_dt[, sale_month := as.yearmon(sale_date)]
sales_dt[, event_time := round((sale_date - move_date)/30.44)] # months

# Treatment within 0.10 mile (=528 ft)
sales_dt[, treat := (dist_ft <= 528 & event_time >= 0)]
# Control: 0.10–0.30 mile
sales_dt[, control_band := (dist_ft > 528 & dist_ft <= 1584)]

# Keep estimation window ±24 months
sales_dt <- sales_dt[event_time >= -24 & event_time <= 24]

# ---------------------------------------------
# 4. Main DiD/Event Study Specification
# Outcome: log real price
feols_main <- feols(log(price) ~ i(event_time, treat, ref = -1) | 
                    parcel_id + month(sale_date) , 
                    data = sales_dt[treat | control_band],
                    cluster = ~ offender_id)

summary(feols_main)

# ---------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: Alternative Ring 0.05 mile & 0.05–0.10 mile
sales_dt[, treat50 := (dist_ft <= 264 & event_time >= 0)]
sales_dt[, control50 := (dist_ft > 264 & dist_ft <= 528)]
feols_rb <- feols(log(price) ~ i(event_time, treat50, ref = -1) |
                  parcel_id + month(sale_date),
                  data = sales_dt[treat50 | control50],
                  cluster = ~ offender_id)
summary(feols_rb)
```

The code:
• Loads CSVs  
• Computes great-circle distances with sf, converts to feet  
• Creates treatment dummy & event-time bins  
• Runs an event study with parcel and month fixed effects (two-way)  
• Clusters at offender level  
• Robustness with narrower rings.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

6. EXPECTED RESULTS  

Economic intuition: Proximity to a sex-offender increases perceived risk of
victimization, especially for households with children. Prior work on crime
gradients suggests 2–8 percent capitalization for salient shocks. I expect:

• Homes within 0.10 mile fall by ≈4 % (≈$5,000 on $125k median in 2004 $).  
• Effect should decay quickly; virtually zero beyond 0.3 mile.  
• Largest drop occurs in first 6–12 months, then partially rebounds if
  offender moves away.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DiD)  
(1 = clearly satisfied; 0 = questionable)

C1: Parallel pre-trends verified………………………………………. 0.8  
C2: Sharp, well-timed treatment shock……………………………. 1  
C3: No interference/spillovers to control group……………… 0.6  
C4: Stable unit composition / no differential selection…… 0.7  
C5: Correct functional form & inference (clustered)……… 0.9  

Average score: 0.8 → Reasonably credible with planned checks.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
